subject: Mixed (Real Weightage)
description: 100 questions following the real PGP-CET 2025 subject weightage. Mix: 1 easy / 73 medium / 26 hard. Every question cites its source.

questions.question: The crystals seen in gouty arthritis are:

options.B: Calcium pyrophosphate (positively birefringent)

questions.explanation: Gout: needle-shaped, negatively birefringent urate crystals; pseudogout: rhomboid, positively birefringent CPPD crystals with chondrocalcinosis (menisci).
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise; Maheshwari, Essential Orthopaedics; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: During the Protection Phase (early, acute stage) of soft tissue injury management, the primary goal is to:

options.B: Control the effects of inflammation (e.g. rest, ice, compression, elevation) while preventing the deleterious effects of complete immobility
options.C: Perform aggressive stretching to end-range regardless of pain
options.D: Discharge the patient with no further intervention needed

questions.explanation: The Protection Phase focuses on controlling inflammation (selective rest, ice, compression, elevation) while also preventing the adverse effects of complete immobilization through careful, nondestructive movement (passive ROM, gentle massage, muscle setting) — balancing protection with the need to avoid stiffness and adhesion formation.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 10: Soft Tissue Injury, Repair, and Management — Management Guidelines, Protection Phase
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: In a patient with a spinal cord injury who lacks active control of the back extensors, why might a therapist deliberately allow mild hypomobility to develop in the low back extensors while still fully stretching the hamstrings?

options.A: To create a stable, slightly shortened structure the patient can lean into for trunk support during long-term sitting
options.B: Because the back extensors cannot physically be stretched
options.C: To prevent contractures developing in the hamstrings only
options.D: Because stretching the trunk has no clinical value in this population

questions.explanation: This illustrates 'selective stretching': deliberately allowing some hypomobility in muscles the patient cannot actively control (like the back extensors after a thoracic/cervical spinal cord injury) gives them a stable structure to lean into for trunk stability while sitting, while the hamstrings are kept flexible enough for dressing and transfers.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 4: Stretching for Impaired Mobility — Selective Stretching
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Exercise Therapy

questions.question: Isolated haemoptysis (coughing up blood), even when the chest radiograph appears normal, may be the first sign of which condition?

options.B: Simple viral upper respiratory tract infection

questions.explanation: Isolated haemoptysis can be the first sign of bronchogenic carcinoma even when the chest X-ray is normal, which is why it should always be taken seriously and investigated further rather than dismissed.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: A Grade 3 (third-degree) soft tissue injury is characterised by:

options.A: Mild pain only within the first 24 hours, with minimal swelling
options.B: Near-complete or complete tear/avulsion of the tissue, often with instability if a ligament is involved, and stress to the tissue being usually painless
options.C: Moderate pain requiring the activity to stop, with some fibers torn
options.D: No pain whatsoever, at any point

questions.explanation: A Grade 3 injury involves near-complete or complete tear/avulsion of the tissue (tendon or ligament); notably, stress to the injured tissue is usually painless (since it's fully torn), and a torn ligament results in joint instability — a key distinguishing feature from Grade 1 and 2 injuries.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 10: Soft Tissue Injury, Repair, and Management — Severity of Tissue Injury
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: Pain over the lateral epicondyle on resisted wrist extension with the elbow extended and forearm pronated (Cozen's test) indicates:

options.B: Radial tunnel only

questions.explanation: Cozen's and Mill's tests stress the common extensor origin (ECRB) to reproduce lateral elbow pain.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels & Worthingham's Muscle Testing; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment; Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: A stroke patient has nonfluent, slow, hesitant speech with a limited vocabulary, but relatively preserved auditory comprehension. This is classically associated with a lesion of:

options.A: Wernicke's area, in the posterior temporal gyrus
options.B: Broca's area, in the third frontal convolution of the dominant hemisphere

questions.explanation: This is classic Broca's (nonfluent, expressive) aphasia — slow, effortful, nonfluent speech with a limited vocabulary but relatively preserved comprehension — caused by a lesion of Broca's area in the dominant (typically left) frontal lobe. Wernicke's (fluent, receptive) aphasia, by contrast, produces fluent but often meaningless speech with impaired comprehension.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Middle Cerebral Artery Syndrome
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: A diagnosis of multiple sclerosis (MS) requires evidence of CNS damage that satisfies which two key criteria?

options.A: Damage in only one CNS location, confirmed once
options.B: Dissemination of lesions in space (at least two separate CNS areas) AND dissemination in time (damage at two separate points at least 1 month apart)
options.C: A single MRI scan showing any abnormality
options.D: Positive family history alone, without any imaging

questions.explanation: MS diagnosis requires evidence of damage in at least two separate areas of the CNS (dissemination in space) occurring at two separate points in time at least 1 month apart (dissemination in time), plus exclusion of other possible diagnoses — as reflected in the revised McDonald Criteria.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: Testing the medial hamstrings in prone requires the hip to be:

options.A: Laterally rotated with the knee extended
options.B: Slightly medially rotated with the knee flexed, resistance on the distal leg

questions.explanation: Medial rotation of the hip with knee flexion isolates semitendinosus and semimembranosus; lateral rotation emphasises biceps femoris.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels & Worthingham's Muscle Testing; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment; Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: The Grotthus–Draper law states that:

options.A: Radiation intensity falls with the square of the distance
options.B: Metabolic rate doubles for each 10 °C rise
options.C: Only radiation that is absorbed by the tissue can produce an effect in it
options.D: Heat produced is proportional to I²Rt

questions.explanation: For any physiological effect, radiation must be absorbed; reflected or transmitted radiation produces no effect.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: The close-packed position of the knee joint is:

options.B: 90° flexion

questions.explanation: Close-packed (maximum congruency and ligament tension): knee full extension; hip extension with medial rotation; elbow extension; shoulder abduction with lateral rotation.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels & Worthingham's Muscle Testing; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment; Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: The FABER (Patrick's) test assesses the:

options.B: Knee collaterals

questions.explanation: Flexion, abduction and external rotation of the hip stress the hip and SI joint; groin pain indicates hip pathology, posterior pain the SI joint.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels & Worthingham's Muscle Testing; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment; Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: Spontaneous fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves at rest on EMG, appearing about 2–3 weeks after injury, indicate:

options.B: Normal muscle

questions.explanation: Denervated muscle fibres become hypersensitive to acetylcholine and fire spontaneously; fibrillations and positive sharp waves are the typical findings at rest.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: A swan-neck deformity of the finger consists of:

options.B: PIP flexion and DIP hyperextension

questions.explanation: Common in rheumatoid arthritis; volar plate laxity at the PIP joint and tight intrinsics produce PIP hyperextension with DIP flexion.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise; Maheshwari, Essential Orthopaedics; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: Lacunar strokes, caused by small penetrating-vessel disease deep in the cerebral white matter, are most strongly associated with which underlying conditions?

options.B: Hypertensive small-vessel disease and diabetic microvascular disease

questions.explanation: Lacunar strokes result from small vessel (penetrating artery) disease deep in the cerebral white matter, and are strongly associated with chronic hypertension and diabetic microvascular disease, producing distinctive syndromes such as pure motor hemiplegia.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: Massive haemoglobin absorption by the renal tubules in severe falciparum malaria produces which complication?

options.B: Cerebral malaria

questions.explanation: In falciparum malaria, massive absorption of haemoglobin (released by destroyed red cells) by the renal tubules produces blackwater fever, also called haemoglobinuric nephrosis.
questions.sourceBook: Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: The Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST) uses which three components to calculate overall risk of undernutrition?

options.A: BMI, recent weight loss, and the acute disease effect (likely absence of nutritional intake)
options.B: Blood pressure, heart rate, and temperature only

questions.explanation: The MUST tool combines three scored components — BMI, percentage weight loss over 3-6 months, and the acute disease effect (adding points if there has been or will likely be little/no nutritional intake for 5+ days) — to classify overall undernutrition risk as low, medium, or high.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Nutritional Assessment — Clinical, The MUST Tool
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: In psoriasis the epidermal transit time is shortened to about:

options.B: 1 hour

questions.explanation: Normal epidermal turnover takes about 28 days (up to 70 including full migration); in psoriasis it is greatly accelerated; UV reduces cell proliferation.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: Morning headaches in a patient with severe respiratory failure may signify:

options.B: Simple dehydration only
options.C: Normal sleep patterns with no pathology

questions.explanation: Morning headaches in patients with severe respiratory failure may signify nocturnal carbon dioxide retention (hypercapnia during sleep), which can be confirmed with early morning arterial blood gases or nocturnal transcutaneous CO2 monitoring.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: Blastomas (embryomas) such as neuroblastoma, nephroblastoma (Wilms' tumour), and retinoblastoma are notable because they:

options.A: Occur almost exclusively in adults over 60
options.B: Arise from embryonal/partially differentiated cells and occur more frequently in infants and children under 5
options.C: Are always benign despite the '-oma' name

questions.explanation: Blastomas arise from embryonal or partially differentiated cells that would normally form the blastema of organs/tissues during embryogenesis, and occur more frequently in infants and children under 5 years of age.
questions.sourceBook: Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: Isolated blunt liver or splenic injury in a haemodynamically stable child is generally best managed by:

options.B: Non-operative management with observation

questions.explanation: Isolated liver or splenic injury in a stable child can usually be managed non-operatively, with laparotomy reserved for ongoing intra-abdominal bleeding; uncomplicated cases can often be discharged after 5-7 days with a period of restricted activity.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — Paediatric Trauma
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: The concept of a 'treatment threshold' in clinical decision-making primarily balances:

options.A: The doctor's personal preference against the hospital's budget
options.B: The risks of testing/waiting against the risks and benefits of starting treatment now
options.C: Only the cost of the test, with no consideration of patient risk
options.D: Nothing — treatment thresholds do not exist in evidence-based medicine

questions.explanation: The treatment threshold combines the risks of a test, and the risks versus benefits of treatment, to decide the point at which it makes sense to act. For a low-risk, effective intervention (e.g. antibiotics for a likely UTI), the threshold to act is lower; for a high-risk intervention, more diagnostic certainty is required first.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Clinical Decision Making — Dealing with Uncertainty
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: In the platelet haemostasis mechanism, thromboxane A2 primarily acts to:

options.B: Further increase platelet aggregation and cause vasoconstriction, helping form the temporary haemostatic plug

questions.explanation: Thromboxane A2 further increases platelet aggregation (along with platelet adhesion, forming the temporary haemostatic plug) and causes vasoconstriction, helping stop bleeding from the injured vessel — the opposite effect to prostacyclin, which inhibits thromboxane A2 formation to keep the platelet plug localized.
questions.sourceBook: AK Jain, Physiology
questions.sourceChapter: Platelets or Thrombocytes — Functions, Blood Coagulation
questions.subject: Physiology

questions.question: Which of the following is a recognised physical complication of a severe, chronic cough?

options.B: Permanent hearing loss

questions.explanation: Chronic, forceful coughing can cause 'cough fractures' of the ribs and hernias, due to the repeated high intra-thoracic and intra-abdominal pressures generated. Stress urinary incontinence is another common, often under-reported complication, especially in women.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: Madelung's deformity results from retarded growth of which structure?

options.A: The lower end of the radius
options.B: The upper end of the humerus
options.C: The olecranon process of the ulna

questions.explanation: Madelung's deformity is a dorsal subluxation (displacement) of the lower end of the ulna, caused by retarded growth of the lower end of the radius.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Clinical Anatomy
questions.subject: Anatomy

questions.question: Back pain that IMPROVES with exercise and worsens with rest, with morning stiffness over 30 minutes in a young male, suggests:

options.B: Mechanical low back strain

questions.explanation: Inflammatory back pain: onset before 40 years, insidious, morning stiffness, improves with exercise, nocturnal pain.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise; Maheshwari, Essential Orthopaedics; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) is a clot-dissolving therapy for acute ischemic stroke. Within what time window from symptom onset must it generally be given to be effective and safe?

options.B: 3 hours

questions.explanation: tPA must generally be given within 3 hours of symptom onset to be effective, and cannot be given in hemorrhagic stroke because it may worsen bleeding — this is why rapid recognition of stroke symptoms and emergency imaging (CT) to distinguish ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke are critical ('time is brain').
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Risk Factors and Stroke Prevention
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: In a patient with acute respiratory distress and suspected pulmonary embolism, what is the significance of a completely NORMAL chest radiograph?

options.B: A normal radiograph does NOT exclude a major pulmonary embolus — in fact, a normal film in a patient with acute respiratory distress is actually suggestive of the diagnosis
options.C: It means the patient definitely has pneumonia instead
options.D: It has no diagnostic relevance whatsoever

questions.explanation: A normal chest radiograph does NOT exclude a major pulmonary embolus. In fact, in a patient presenting with acute respiratory distress, a normal-appearing radiograph is actually suggestive of pulmonary embolism as the underlying diagnosis, since conventional radiographic findings in PE are nonspecific (or absent).
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: Which of the following is a NORMAL, physiological example of apoptosis rather than a pathological one?

options.A: Cell death in tumours exposed to chemotherapy
options.B: Regression of the lactating breast after breastfeeding is withdrawn

questions.explanation: Physiologic apoptosis includes organised tissue sculpting during embryonic development, hormone-dependent tissue involution (such as regression of the lactating breast after weaning, or endometrial shedding), and normal replacement proliferation in tissues like intestinal epithelium — distinct from pathological apoptosis, such as chemotherapy-induced tumour cell death.
questions.sourceBook: Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology
questions.sourceChapter: Cell Injury, Cellular Adaptations and Cellular Ageing — Apoptosis in Biologic Processes
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: For a very painful, irritable joint, the most appropriate Maitland mobilisation is:

options.A: Grade IV at the end of range
options.B: Prolonged stretch to maximum tolerance
options.C: Grade I–II oscillations, within the pain-free range

questions.explanation: Gentle low-grade oscillations stimulate mechanoreceptors and inhibit pain (gate control) without provoking the irritable tissue.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels & Worthingham's Muscle Testing; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment; Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: A contrast bath in the upper or lower limb is traditionally applied as:

options.B: 30 seconds hot and 10 seconds cold
options.D: About 3–4 minutes of warm immersion alternating with about 1 minute of cold

questions.explanation: Alternating vasodilatation and vasoconstriction (the ‘pump’ effect) is thought to help in subacute oedema and stiffness; the usual ratio is 4:1 hot:cold.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: Chronic pain syndrome, as distinguished from ordinary chronic inflammation, is defined as a state that:

options.A: Persists longer than 6 months, with pain that cannot be linked to an identifiable source of irritation or inflammation, and includes physical, emotional, and psychosocial functional limitations
options.B: Always resolves completely within 48 hours
options.C: Is defined purely by the presence of visible swelling
options.D: Only ever occurs immediately after acute injury, never later

questions.explanation: Chronic pain syndrome persists longer than 6 months, includes pain that cannot be linked to an identifiable source of ongoing irritation or inflammation, and encompasses functional limitations and disability across physical, emotional, and psychosocial dimensions — distinct from simple chronic inflammation from ongoing tissue irritation.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 10: Soft Tissue Injury, Repair, and Management — Chronic Pain Syndrome
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: Continuous Passive Motion (CPM) is best described as:

options.A: An exercise in which the patient actively moves a joint against resistance
options.B: A mechanical device that moves a joint slowly and continuously through a controlled range of motion, without effort from the patient
options.C: A manual stretching technique applied by the therapist at end-range
options.D: A functional movement pattern combining several joints at once

questions.explanation: CPM refers specifically to a mechanical device that passively and continuously moves a joint through a set arc of motion, developed following Robert Salter's research into the healing benefits of continual passive movement on joint tissue.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 3: Range of Motion — Continuous Passive Motion
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Exercise Therapy

questions.question: A key reason K+ efflux is not fully compensated by Na+ influx at rest (helping maintain the resting membrane potential) is that:

options.A: The resting membrane is much less permeable to Na+ than to K+
options.B: There is no Na+ present in the extracellular fluid at rest
options.C: K+ cannot actually cross the membrane at rest
options.D: Na+ and K+ have identical permeabilities at rest

questions.explanation: Because the resting membrane is much less permeable to Na+ than to K+, the modest inward leak of Na+ does not offset the outward diffusion of K+ down its concentration gradient — contributing to the net negative charge that develops inside the cell at rest.
questions.sourceBook: AK Jain, Physiology
questions.sourceChapter: The Membrane Potentials — Genesis of Resting Membrane Potential
questions.subject: Physiology

questions.question: A BMI below which threshold is associated with significant hospital mortality risk?
questions.explanation: A BMI of less than 18.5 indicates nutritional impairment, but a BMI below 15 specifically is associated with significant hospital mortality risk.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Nutritional Assessment — Body Weight and Anthropometry
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: A patent processus vaginalis that allows peritoneal fluid (but no bowel) to track down into the scrotum results in:

options.B: A hydrocoele

questions.explanation: When a patent processus vaginalis allows only peritoneal fluid (not bowel) to track into the scrotum, the result is a hydrocoele — typically a non-tender, transilluminating scrotal swelling, distinct from an inguinal hernia where bowel or other abdominal content is present.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: Damage to Wernicke's area, located in the left temporal lobe, characteristically produces speech that is:

options.A: Completely absent — the patient cannot make any sound
options.B: Fluent in output but conveying little actual meaning, with impaired understanding of speech and written language
options.C: Slow and effortful but perfectly meaningful
options.D: Normal in every respect except pitch

questions.explanation: Wernicke's area damage markedly impairs comprehension of spoken and written language. Characteristically, the patient's own speech remains fluent in its flow and rhythm but conveys little coherent meaning.
questions.sourceBook: Morgan & King, Introduction to Psychology
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Temporal-Lobe Association Cortex, Language Functions
questions.subject: Psychology

questions.question: High-voltage pulsed current (HVPC) is best described as:

options.A: A symmetrical biphasic square wave of long duration
options.B: A continuous direct current of low voltage
options.C: A twin-peak, monophasic pulse of very short duration with a low average current

questions.explanation: HVPC has a very high peak voltage (>150 V) but very short pulses (about 5–20 µs), so the average current is small and comfortable; it is used for oedema, wound healing and pain.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: Which of the following is cited as a genuine limitation of mortality data, particularly relevant to developing countries like India?

options.A: Incomplete reporting of deaths and lack of accuracy in recording age/cause of death
options.B: Mortality data is always 100% complete and accurate worldwide
options.C: Death certificates do not exist in any country
options.D: Mortality data cannot be tabulated by any coding system

questions.explanation: Incomplete reporting of deaths is not usually a problem in developed countries, but can be considerable in India and other developing countries. Combined with inaccuracies in age/cause recording (often due to lack of diagnostic evidence, inexperienced certifying doctors, or absence of postmortem examination), this is a genuine limitation of mortality data quality.
questions.sourceBook: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Measurement of Mortality — Limitations of Mortality Data
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Community Health

questions.question: A neuropathic (Charcot) joint is typically:

options.A: Associated with severe pain at rest
options.B: Painless, swollen and unstable

questions.explanation: Loss of pain/proprioception leads to repeated trauma; most common cause is diabetes (foot/ankle); also syphilis, syringomyelia, leprosy.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise; Maheshwari, Essential Orthopaedics; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: Which hormone is chiefly responsible for the 'milk ejection' or 'let-down' reflex during breastfeeding?

options.B: Oxytocin

questions.explanation: Oxytocin is the major galactokinetic hormone: suckling triggers a neural reflex arc to the hypothalamus, causing oxytocin release from the posterior pituitary, which contracts the myoepithelial cells around the alveoli and ducts, forcing milk down into the lactiferous ducts (the 'let-down' reflex). Prolactin, by contrast, drives milk secretion itself (lactogenesis/galactopoiesis), not its ejection.
questions.sourceBook: Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Physiology of Lactation, Galactokinesis
questions.subject: OBGY

questions.question: The energy absorbed or released when a substance changes state without a change in temperature is called:

options.B: Specific heat

questions.explanation: Latent heat is the energy needed for a change of state (e.g. water to vapour); it explains the cooling effect of vapocoolant sprays and evaporation.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: In managing spasticity in MS patients, why must a therapist be cautious about excessive pharmacological reduction of spasticity in some patients?

options.A: Spasticity has no functional role and should always be eliminated completely
options.B: Spasticity can sometimes be functionally useful (e.g. extensor spasticity assisting standing during a stand-pivot transfer), so over-reducing it may cause loss of function
options.C: Antispasticity medications have no side effects to worry about
options.D: Spasticity always improves function no matter how severe

questions.explanation: While excessive spasticity impairs function, spasticity can sometimes substitute for lost strength — for example, extensor spasticity assisting a patient during a stand-pivot transfer. Significant pharmacological reduction of spasticity in such cases could therefore paradoxically worsen functional performance.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 16: Multiple Sclerosis — Management of Symptoms, Spasticity
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: The minimum and maximum scores on the Glasgow Coma Scale are:

options.B: 3 and 15

questions.explanation: GCS = eye (1–4) + verbal (1–5) + motor (1–6) = 3–15; ≤8 is severe brain injury.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels & Worthingham's Muscle Testing; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment; Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: What is the general relationship between the intensity (load) of resistance exercise and the number of repetitions/sets possible?

options.A: There is no relationship — repetitions are independent of load
options.B: An inverse relationship: higher intensity/load permits fewer repetitions and sets, and lower load permits more
options.C: A direct relationship: higher load always allows more repetitions
options.D: Repetitions only depend on the patient's age, never on the load used

questions.explanation: There is an inverse relationship between exercise intensity (load) and the number of repetitions/sets possible — the higher the load, the fewer repetitions and sets that can be performed, and vice versa.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: A woman who delivers twins in her first pregnancy is correctly recorded as:

options.B: Gravida 1, Para 1

questions.explanation: Gravida and para refer to PREGNANCIES, not the number of babies delivered. A woman delivering twins in her first pregnancy is still gravida one, para one — parity is not increased by multiple fetuses in a single pregnancy.
questions.sourceBook: Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics
questions.sourceChapter: Antenatal Care — History Taking, Vital Statistics
questions.subject: OBGY

questions.question: Activation of a Gi-coupled receptor typically has which effect on adenylyl cyclase and cAMP?

options.B: Inhibits adenylyl cyclase, decreasing cAMP
options.C: Has no effect on adenylyl cyclase, acts only on phospholipase C

questions.explanation: Gi (inhibitory G-protein) inhibits adenylyl cyclase, lowering intracellular cAMP — the opposite of Gs, which activates adenylyl cyclase and raises cAMP. This is why, for example, muscarinic M2 receptor stimulation (Gi-coupled) in the heart opposes the effect of beta-adrenergic (Gs-coupled) stimulation.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Mechanism of Drug Action; Receptor Pharmacology
questions.subject: Pharmacology

questions.question: In behavioural treatment of anorexia nervosa aimed at weight gain, what is the recommended maximum safe rate of weight gain?

options.B: 10 kg per week
options.C: There is no upper limit — faster is always better

questions.explanation: Weight gain in anorexia nervosa treatment should not exceed 1.5 to 2 kg per fortnight — too-rapid weight gain is considered neither desirable nor safe, and patients are often encouraged to eat smaller, more frequent meals (around six per day) rather than large ones.
questions.sourceBook: Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry
questions.subject: Psychiatry

questions.question: What is the key limitation of Sanger's reagent (1-fluoro-2,4-dinitrobenzene) compared to Edman's reagent for determining a protein's amino acid sequence?

options.A: It only works on carbohydrates, not proteins
options.B: After labelling the N-terminal residue, the protein must be fully hydrolysed to identify it — destroying the polypeptide and preventing repeated sequencing cycles
options.C: It cannot label any amino acid at all
options.D: It is more expensive but otherwise functionally identical to Edman's reagent

questions.explanation: Sanger's reagent labels the free N-terminal amino group, but identifying that labelled residue requires complete hydrolysis of the protein — destroying it in the process. This makes it useful only for identifying the N-terminal residue once, unlike Edman degradation which can be repeated.
questions.sourceBook: Satyanarayana, Biochemistry
questions.sourceChapter: Proteins and Amino Acids — Determination of Primary Structure
questions.subject: Biochemistry

questions.question: How is musculoskeletal (chest wall) pain typically distinguished from pleuritic pain on physical examination?

options.A: Musculoskeletal pain is reproduced by palpation, while pleuritic pain is not
options.B: Both are always identical and cannot be distinguished clinically
options.C: Pleuritic pain is always reproduced by palpation, musculoskeletal pain never is
options.D: Musculoskeletal pain never worsens with movement

questions.explanation: Musculoskeletal (chest wall) pain is usually well localized and its reproduction on palpation is a key distinguishing clinical feature — pleuritic pain, by contrast, is not reproduced by palpation.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: In Adult Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS), what is emphasised as more diagnostically useful than the radiographic appearance alone?

options.A: The timing of the radiographic changes relative to the insult and onset of symptoms
options.B: The patient's blood type
options.C: The exact colour of the consolidation on the film
options.D: The time of day the X-ray was taken

questions.explanation: In ARDS, it is the TIMING of radiographic changes relative to the inciting insult and the onset of clinical symptoms — rather than the radiological appearance alone (which resembles pulmonary oedema) — that helps suggest the diagnosis, since the chest radiograph is often normal in the initial hours despite clinical distress.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Thoracic Imaging — Adult Respiratory Distress Syndrome
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: Cerebral edema following ischemic stroke typically reaches its maximum at approximately what time point, and is the most frequent cause of death in acute stroke?

options.B: 3 to 4 days

questions.explanation: Cerebral edema begins within minutes of the ischemic insult and reaches its maximum by 3 to 4 days, gradually subsiding by 2 to 3 weeks. Significant edema, particularly with large MCA/ICA infarcts, is the most frequent cause of death in acute stroke due to raised intracranial pressure and brainstem herniation.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: A disease that was previously known and thought to have been controlled or eradicated, but has now reappeared, is termed:

options.B: A re-emerging disease

questions.explanation: An emerging infectious disease is one newly appearing in a population or increasing in incidence/range. If the disease was previously known and thought controlled or eradicated but reappears, it is specifically termed re-emerging.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Epidemiology of Infection — Emerging and Re-emerging Disease
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: Training to improve muscular (local) endurance typically involves:

options.A: A very heavy load for only 1-2 repetitions
options.B: Many repetitions (e.g. 3-5 sets of 40-50 reps) against a low, submaximal load
options.C: A single maximal isometric contraction held for 1 second
options.D: Complete rest with no muscular activity

questions.explanation: Muscle endurance training involves performing many repetitions against a submaximal load — for example, as many as three to five sets of 40 to 50 repetitions against a low resistance — and can be safely initiated early in rehabilitation since the load involved is low.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — To Improve Muscle Endurance
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: Corticosteroid use weakening host defence mechanisms and allowing reactivation of latent tuberculosis is an example of which category of adverse drug effect?

options.B: A secondary effect (an indirect consequence of the drug's primary action)

questions.explanation: Secondary effects are indirect consequences of a drug's primary action — corticosteroids' primary immunosuppressive action indirectly allows latent infections like tuberculosis to reactivate, and similarly, tetracyclines suppressing normal bacterial flora can indirectly permit superinfections.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.subject: Pharmacology

questions.question: In the long bones of the upper limb, the 'growing ends' (which fuse with the shaft latest) are located at which joints?

options.B: Shoulder and wrist joints
options.D: All joints fuse at exactly the same time

questions.explanation: By the law of ossification, the epiphysis that appears first at a given end fuses last. In the upper limb this means the upper end of the humerus and the lower ends of both the radius and ulna are the 'growing ends' — they fuse with their shafts later than the corresponding opposite ends.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Ossification
questions.subject: Anatomy

questions.question: To achieve full passive range of hip flexion, the knee must also be allowed to flex. Why?

options.A: It relaxes tension on the two-joint hamstring muscle group, which would otherwise restrict hip flexion
options.B: It reduces pain in the lumbar spine
options.C: It is required purely to stabilize the pelvis
options.D: Knee position has no real effect on hip flexion range

questions.explanation: The hamstrings cross both the hip and knee. Keeping the knee extended while flexing the hip stretches the hamstrings and limits how far the hip can flex; flexing the knee releases that tension, allowing full hip flexion range to be reached.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 3: Range of Motion — Combined Hip and Knee Motion
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Exercise Therapy

questions.question: Why is establishing a 1-RM (single maximum effort) considered inappropriate for certain patient populations, such as those with osteoporosis or cardiovascular pathology?

options.A: It takes too long to administer in a clinical setting
options.B: It requires a single maximal effort, which carries risk for patients with joint impairments, healing soft tissue, osteoporosis, or cardiovascular pathology
options.C: It is only valid for measuring endurance, not strength
options.D: It cannot be performed using free weights

questions.explanation: A 1-RM test requires the patient to exert one true maximal effort, which is unsafe for patients with joint impairments, those recovering from or at risk of soft tissue injury, or those with osteoporosis or cardiovascular pathology — alternative methods (e.g. multiple-RM formulas, dynamometry, percentage of body weight) are used instead for these patients.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Repetition Maximum, Precautions
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: On a chest radiograph, emphysema characteristically produces overinflation of the lungs, flattening of the diaphragm, and:

options.A: An enlarged, apparently big heart with an increased cardiothoracic ratio
options.B: An apparently SMALL heart with a DECREASED cardiothoracic ratio, due to diaphragmatic flattening
options.C: Complete absence of any pulmonary vessels
options.D: No change to the appearance of the diaphragm

questions.explanation: In emphysema, overinflation of the lungs flattens the diaphragmatic dome, which results in an apparently small heart and a decreased cardiothoracic ratio on the chest radiograph — along with 'pruning' of the pulmonary vessels and, on lateral film, a large retrosternal translucency.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Thoracic Imaging — Chronic Airflow Limitation, Emphysema
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: The medial meniscus is injured more commonly than the lateral meniscus because it is:

options.B: Less mobile, being attached to the medial collateral ligament and joint capsule

questions.explanation: The medial meniscus is firmly attached to the deep MCL and capsule, so it is less able to move away from compression and rotation forces.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise; Maheshwari, Essential Orthopaedics; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: A burn destroying the entire epidermis and dermis with damage to subcutaneous tissue is classified as:

options.B: First-degree

questions.explanation: Full-thickness burns are painless, leathery and need grafting.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise; Maheshwari, Essential Orthopaedics; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: In the rehabilitation framework for MS, which category of impairment is described as generally NOT responsive to intervention, in contrast to indirect impairments caused by inactivity/disuse (which CAN be modified)?

options.A: Direct CNS impairments (from the disease process itself)
options.B: Decreased muscle endurance from disuse

questions.explanation: Direct CNS impairments caused by the MS disease process itself are not responsive to rehabilitative intervention, whereas INDIRECT impairments from inactivity and disuse (decreased muscle endurance, osteoporosis, cardiovascular deconditioning) can be meaningfully improved — for example, strength training can improve balance and gait despite the underlying CNS damage remaining unchanged.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 16: Multiple Sclerosis — Framework for Rehabilitation
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: In an ERECT chest radiograph, the first and most important radiographic sign of elevated left ventricular pressure (early left ventricular failure) is:

options.A: Upper lobe blood diversion (shunting of blood to the upper zones)
options.B: A completely normal-appearing chest X-ray in all cases
options.C: Immediate cavitation of the lung fields

questions.explanation: As left atrial pressure rises, blood is shunted to the upper zones — upper lobe blood diversion — which is the first and most important radiographic sign of elevated left ventricular pressure on an erect film. This sign cannot be reliably assessed on a supine radiograph due to redistribution of blood flow in that position.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: Interrupted direct current of long pulse duration is used mainly to stimulate:

options.A: Nerve roots for pain gate control
options.B: Normal innervated muscle for strengthening

questions.explanation: Denervated muscle has a higher chronaxie and needs long-duration pulses (tens to hundreds of ms) of adequate intensity to contract.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: The 'blue dot sign' on the scrotum in a boy just before puberty is classically associated with:

options.B: Torsion of a testicular/epididymal appendage (hydatid of Morgagni)

questions.explanation: Torsion of a testicular or epididymal appendage (hydatid of Morgagni) characteristically affects boys just before puberty, and the torted, infarcted appendage may occasionally be visible or palpable through the scrotal skin as a tender bluish nodule — the 'blue dot sign'.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — The Acute Scrotum
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: Following moderate-intensity resistance training, what rest period is generally recommended between sets?

options.B: 2 to 3 minutes
options.D: No rest is needed between sets

questions.explanation: For moderate-intensity resistance training, a 2- to 3-minute rest period between sets is generally recommended, with longer rest periods (>3 minutes) needed for high-intensity training of large, multi-joint muscle groups.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: Mortality statistics are described as 'virtually useless' for studying which category of disease?

options.A: Diseases with very high fatality rates
options.B: Diseases with low fatality, such as mental diseases or arthritis

questions.explanation: Mortality data are virtually useless for studying diseases associated with low fatality, such as mental diseases or arthritis, since these conditions rarely appear as a cause of death even though they cause significant morbidity — morbidity data are needed instead for such conditions.
questions.sourceBook: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Measurement of Mortality — Limitations of Mortality Data
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Community Health

questions.question: 'ROWS' (Rule Out Worst-case Scenario) as a clinical strategy is best illustrated by which example?

options.A: Assuming pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness is always a pulled muscle
options.B: Actively investigating for pulmonary embolism in a patient presenting with pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness, because missing it could be fatal
options.C: Ignoring red flag symptoms in back pain to save time
options.D: Only used for patients over 65 years old

questions.explanation: ROWS forces clinicians to actively consider and rule out serious, potentially fatal diagnoses that can present with common symptoms — the classic textbook example is investigating for pulmonary embolism in a patient with pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Clinical Decision Making — Red Flags and ROWS
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: Which of the following is a correct characteristic of the peptide bond?

options.A: It is highly flexible and freely rotates
options.B: It is rigid and planar, with partial double-bond character, generally existing in the trans configuration
options.C: It cannot participate in hydrogen bonding
options.D: It only forms between two acidic amino acids

questions.explanation: The peptide bond (C=O to N-H) has partial double-bond character, which makes it rigid and planar rather than freely rotating, and it generally exists in the trans configuration. Both the C=O and N-H groups are polar and participate in hydrogen bond formation, which is important for secondary structure.
questions.sourceBook: Satyanarayana, Biochemistry
questions.sourceChapter: Proteins and Amino Acids — Peptide Bond
questions.subject: Biochemistry

questions.question: Early ambulation after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery is encouraged mainly because it:

options.A: Has no measurable benefit but is traditional practice
options.B: Reduces bladder complications and constipation, facilitates uterine drainage, and lessens the risk of puerperal venous thrombosis and embolism
options.D: Prevents postpartum haemorrhage entirely on its own

questions.explanation: Early ambulation after delivery provides a sense of well-being, reduces bladder complications and constipation, facilitates uterine drainage (hastening involution), and importantly lessens the risk of puerperal venous thrombosis and embolism.
questions.sourceBook: Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Management, Rest and Ambulation
questions.subject: OBGY

questions.question: Unlike necrosis, apoptosis is characteristically NOT accompanied by:

options.B: Inflammation and collateral tissue damage
options.C: Cell membrane changes of any kind
options.D: Any regulation by the cell itself

questions.explanation: Apoptosis is a controlled, internally programmed form of cell death ('cell suicide') that, unlike necrosis, occurs without triggering inflammation or collateral tissue damage — this is one of the key distinguishing features between the two forms of cell death.
questions.sourceBook: Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology
questions.sourceChapter: Cell Injury, Cellular Adaptations and Cellular Ageing — Apoptosis
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: The maximum weight which can safely be used with skin traction is about:

options.B: 5 kg

questions.explanation: Skin traction relies on adhesive or non-adhesive bandages and cannot withstand more than about 4–5 kg without skin damage; skeletal traction is used for heavier forces.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise; Maheshwari, Essential Orthopaedics; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: Mechanical cervical traction to separate the posterior elements (e.g. facet joints, foramen) is usually applied with the neck positioned in:

options.B: Full lateral flexion

questions.explanation: Moderate flexion opens the intervertebral foramina and posterior joints most effectively; extension would compress them.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: Peripheral oedema in a respiratory patient most commonly suggests which underlying process?

options.A: Right heart failure, potentially due to cor pulmonale (right ventricular failure secondary to hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction)
options.B: Left ventricular failure exclusively
options.C: Normal ageing with no pathological significance

questions.explanation: Peripheral oedema in a respiratory patient suggests right heart failure, which may result from cor pulmonale — right ventricular failure secondary to hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction from underlying chronic lung disease. It can also occur from salt/water retention with high-dose corticosteroid use.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: Which of the following is a documented benefit of Continuous Passive Motion (CPM) following joint surgery?

options.A: A permanent increase in muscle strength
options.B: Increased synovial fluid lubrication and a stimulating effect on healing of cartilage, tendons, and ligaments
options.C: It removes the need for any active exercise afterward

questions.explanation: Documented benefits of CPM include increased synovial fluid lubrication (supporting cartilage healing), a stimulating effect on tendon and ligament healing, prevention of adhesions/contractures, and typically a quicker return of range of motion with less postoperative pain — but it does not replace active exercise or strength training.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 3: Range of Motion — Continuous Passive Motion
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Exercise Therapy

questions.question: High fevers occurring specifically at night, associated with night sweats, may be an early indicator of which condition?

options.B: Pulmonary tuberculosis

questions.explanation: High fevers occurring at night with associated night sweats may be the first indicator of pulmonary tuberculosis, and should prompt further investigation.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: The lateral intermuscular septum of the thigh, the thickest of the three septa, separates which two compartments?

options.A: The anterior compartment from the posterior compartment
options.B: The medial compartment from the posterior compartment
options.C: The anterior compartment from the medial compartment
options.D: It does not separate any compartments

questions.explanation: The lateral intermuscular septum, the thickest of the thigh's three intermuscular septa, extends from the iliotibial tract to the lateral lip of the linea aspera and separates the anterior compartment of the thigh from the posterior compartment.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Lower Limb
questions.subject: Anatomy

questions.question: Chronaxie is defined as the:

options.A: Longest pulse duration the muscle can tolerate
options.B: Frequency at which tetanus occurs
options.C: Intensity required for a 1 ms pulse
options.D: Shortest pulse duration needed to excite the tissue at an intensity of twice the rheobase

questions.explanation: Chronaxie is a measure of tissue excitability; it is much longer in denervated muscle than in normal innervated muscle.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: For measuring elbow flexion with a universal goniometer, the axis is placed over the:

options.B: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus

questions.explanation: Fixed arm along the humerus toward the acromion, moving arm along the radius toward the radial styloid, axis at the lateral epicondyle.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels & Worthingham's Muscle Testing; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment; Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: Joule's law states that the heat produced in a conductor is proportional to:

options.B: The voltage divided by the time
options.C: The square of the current, the resistance and the time (I²Rt)
options.D: The square of the resistance and the current

questions.explanation: Heat = I² × R × t. This is why a high-resistance skin interface heats under electrodes and why doubling the current quadruples the heating.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: Lesions of the parietal lobe of the NONDOMINANT (typically right) hemisphere in MCA syndrome typically produce which type of deficit?

options.B: Perceptual deficits such as unilateral neglect, anosognosia, and spatial disorganization
options.D: Loss of the sense of smell only

questions.explanation: While dominant (usually left) hemisphere parieto-occipital lesions typically produce aphasia, lesions of the nondominant (usually right) parietal lobe typically produce perceptual deficits: unilateral neglect, anosognosia (denial of deficit), apraxia, and spatial disorganization.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Middle Cerebral Artery Syndrome
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: Tinel's sign is elicited by:

options.B: Passive stretch of a muscle
options.C: Percussing over a nerve to produce tingling in its distribution

questions.explanation: A positive Tinel's (distal tingling on percussion) marks a regenerating nerve front or a compressed nerve (e.g. carpal tunnel).
questions.sourceBook: Daniels & Worthingham's Muscle Testing; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment; Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: The femoral triangle is bounded laterally by the medial border of the sartorius and medially by the medial border of the:

options.B: Gracilis

questions.explanation: The femoral triangle is bounded laterally by the medial border of sartorius and medially by the medial border of adductor longus, with its base formed by the inguinal ligament and its apex (directed downward) continuous with the adductor canal.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Lower Limb
questions.subject: Anatomy

questions.question: Which of the following is a recognised cause of thrombocytopenia (decreased platelet count)?

options.B: Hypersplenism (overactivity of the spleen)
options.C: Administration of epinephrine causing splenic contraction

questions.explanation: Hypersplenism (an overactive spleen) is a cause of thrombocytopenia, along with bone marrow depression, certain viral infections (e.g. dengue, which particularly attacks platelets), and drug hypersensitivity. By contrast, splenectomy, epinephrine-induced splenic contraction, and trauma/surgery are causes of thrombocytosis (increased platelet count) — the opposite direction.
questions.sourceBook: AK Jain, Physiology
questions.sourceChapter: Platelets or Thrombocytes — Count and Variations
questions.subject: Physiology

questions.question: In MS, a 'dyssynergic' bladder refers to a problem where:

options.A: The bladder is simply too small to store any urine
options.B: There is a coordination problem between bladder (detrusor) contraction and sphincter relaxation
options.C: The bladder never contracts under any circumstances

questions.explanation: A dyssynergic bladder represents a coordination problem between bladder contraction and sphincter relaxation, distinct from a small spastic bladder (failure to store) or a flaccid/big bladder (failure to empty) — both of which are other recognised patterns of MS-related bladder dysfunction.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: In studying road traffic accidents, why might 'accidents per 1000 vehicles' or 'per million vehicle-miles' be a more useful denominator than total population?

options.A: Total population is always the best denominator regardless of context
options.B: Because many people in the total population do not own or use vehicles, so vehicle-based denominators better reflect actual exposure/risk
options.C: Vehicle-based denominators are only used for aesthetic reasons with no analytical value
options.D: Total population data is impossible to obtain in any country

questions.explanation: When the denominator is more closely related to actual exposure to risk (like the number of vehicles or vehicle-miles travelled) rather than the whole population — many of whom may not drive or use vehicles at all — the resulting rate more accurately reflects the true risk of the event being measured.
questions.sourceBook: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Epidemiology and Epidemiologic Methods — Rates Related to Total Events
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Community Health

questions.question: In the acute stage of myositis ossificans, treatment should include:

options.A: Rest/immobilisation, avoiding massage and forced passive stretching
options.B: Forced passive stretching

questions.explanation: Forced stretching and massage aggravate bleeding and bone formation. Active pain-free movement is introduced only after the acute phase subsides.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise; Maheshwari, Essential Orthopaedics; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: In the 'dual process theory' of clinical reasoning, 'Type 1' thinking is best described as:

options.B: Intuitive, fast, automatic, and pattern-recognition based, but more vulnerable to error
options.D: A thinking style with no relevance to medical practice

questions.explanation: Type 1 thinking is intuitive, heuristic, automatic, fast, and effortless — highly efficient (used in roughly 95% of daily decisions) but more vulnerable to error and more affected by context than Type 2 thinking, which is slow, deliberate, and analytical.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Clinical Decision Making — Type 1 and Type 2 Thinking
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: In the 'ischemic penumbra' surrounding the core of an acute ischemic stroke, neurons:

options.A: Die immediately within seconds, identical to the ischemic core
options.B: Survive for a somewhat longer period than core neurons, but will die without timely reperfusion — making this tissue a key target for acute treatment
options.C: Are completely unaffected by the stroke

questions.explanation: While neurons in the ischemic core die within minutes, the surrounding penumbra contains neurons that survive somewhat longer but remain at risk — cell survival depends on the severity and duration of ischemia, and without timely reperfusion, cells in the penumbra will die and the infarct will expand. This makes the penumbra the key target of emergency stroke treatment.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis typically presents in:

options.A: An obese adolescent boy with hip or referred knee pain
options.B: A neonate

questions.explanation: SUFE occurs at puberty, often overweight; the leg lies externally rotated and shortened. Always examine the hip when a teenager complains of knee pain.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise; Maheshwari, Essential Orthopaedics; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: Why is serum albumin considered an unreliable direct measure of a patient's nutritional status, especially in the acute setting?

options.A: Albumin levels never change regardless of nutrition or illness
options.B: Hypoalbuminaemia often results from altered body fluid composition and increased capillary permeability related to sepsis, not nutrition alone
options.C: Albumin can only be measured once per year
options.D: Albumin is only produced by the kidneys, unrelated to nutrition

questions.explanation: Although a low serum albumin (<30 g/L) is a poor prognostic indicator, hypoalbuminaemia is frequently driven by alterations in body fluid composition and increased capillary permeability from ongoing sepsis or illness — not purely by nutritional intake — so albumin is not a reliable direct marker of nutritional status, particularly acutely.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: In outbreak investigation, a study comparing the recent activities (potential exposures) of affected 'cases' against unaffected 'controls' is called a:

options.B: Randomised controlled trial

questions.explanation: A case-control study compares the recent activities and potential exposures of affected 'cases' to those of unaffected 'controls', helping to identify the likely source of an outbreak.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Epidemiology of Infection — Outbreaks of Infection
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: According to Lambert's cosine law, absorption of radiation at a surface is maximal when the rays strike it:

options.B: Through a mirror only
options.D: At right angles (perpendicular) to the surface

questions.explanation: Maximum intensity is received when the beam is perpendicular to the surface; reduces with the cosine of the angle of incidence.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: The 'incubation period' of an infectious disease is defined as:

options.A: The time between exposure to a pathogen and the development of symptoms
options.B: The total duration of the illness from start to full recovery
options.C: The time a patient spends in hospital
options.D: The period during which a vaccine remains effective

questions.explanation: The incubation period is the time between exposure to a pathogen and the development of symptoms — distinct from the 'period of infectivity', which is the time after exposure during which the patient can transmit the infection to others.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Epidemiology of Infection — Transmission of Infection
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: The carpal tunnel contains the median nerve and:

options.B: The ulnar nerve and artery
options.C: Flexor carpi radialis and palmaris longus tendons

questions.explanation: Nine tendons plus the median nerve pass beneath the flexor retinaculum. Ulnar nerve and artery pass in Guyon's canal.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise; Maheshwari, Essential Orthopaedics; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: 'Passive flexibility' (passive range of motion) is best described as:

options.A: The degree to which an active muscle contraction moves a joint through its available range
options.B: The degree to which a body segment can be moved through its available range by an external force, without the patient contracting the muscle themselves
options.C: The absolute maximum range any joint could reach under general anesthesia
options.D: A measure of muscular endurance during repeated contractions

questions.explanation: Passive flexibility depends on the extensibility of the muscles and connective tissues crossing a joint. It is a prerequisite for, but does not guarantee, dynamic (active) flexibility — which instead depends on the patient's own active muscle contraction moving the segment.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 4: Stretching for Impaired Mobility — Definition of Terms
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Exercise Therapy

questions.question: The classic faradic-type current used to stimulate normal innervated muscle consists of:

options.B: Short-duration (<1 ms) pulses repeated at about 50–100 per second
options.C: Long-duration pulses (>100 ms) repeated once per second

questions.explanation: Faradic-type current uses short pulses to stimulate the motor nerve, producing tetanic contraction at 50–100 Hz. It is unsuitable for denervated muscle.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: In epidemiological terminology, a 'variate' that can only be present or absent (e.g. lung cancer, a broken leg) is described as:

options.B: Discrete
options.D: Non-measurable and therefore not usable in epidemiology

questions.explanation: A variate (any piece of information about a patient or their disease) can be discrete — present or absent, like lung cancer or a broken leg — or continuously distributed, like blood pressure, serum cholesterol, or height. A 'circumstance' is a distinct concept: any environmental factor suspected of causing a disease, such as air pollution.
questions.sourceBook: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Epidemiology and Epidemiologic Methods — Basic Measurements in Epidemiology
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Community Health

questions.question: On the International Death Certificate, Part II records:

options.A: The direct/immediate cause of death only
options.B: Other significant conditions that contributed to the death but were not directly related to the disease or condition causing it
options.D: Only conditions unrelated to the patient's death in any way

questions.explanation: Part II of the death certificate records other significant associated conditions that contributed to the death but did not directly lead to it (e.g. diabetes as a contributing but non-causal condition), distinct from Part I, which records the direct cause and the underlying/antecedent causes forming the direct chain to death.
questions.sourceBook: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Measurement of Mortality — International Death Certificate
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Community Health

questions.question: Why does ischaemia (reduced blood/oxygen supply) lead to cell swelling and damage?

options.A: Ischaemia has no effect on the Na+-K+ pump
options.B: Ischaemia decreases Na+-K+ pump activity, disrupting osmotic equilibrium and allowing the cell to swell
options.C: Ischaemia directly ruptures the cell membrane through mechanical force
options.D: Ischaemia only affects extracellular fluid, never intracellular volume

questions.explanation: The Na+-K+ pump normally keeps osmotic equilibrium by moving positive charge (and effectively solute) out of the cell, counteracting the tendency of intracellular protein anions and other molecules to draw water in and cause swelling. Ischaemia reduces the ATP-dependent pump's activity, disrupting this balance — which is why prolonged cerebral ischaemia, causing cell swelling and damage, is often fatal.
questions.sourceBook: AK Jain, Physiology
questions.subject: Physiology
